Thick and heavy specimen. Compare with Z# 33694 , 189825 , 189826 and 189860 . Metal composition is : Cu 89.1810, Zn 0.3187, Sn 3.7445, As 0.7834, Sb 0.9928, Pb 2.7717, Fe 0.1788, Mn 1.7085, Ni 0.3105, Cd,Co,Bi all are under detection limits, Sum 99.9899 %, XRF data. So we see As-Sb bearing, low led and low tin bronze. Manganese content may be connected with attempts of previous owner to darken the coin with using of KMnO4+CuSO4 solution. Patination is sulphide type - in some points sulphur content reach up to 3 %.

Compare with Z# 33693 , 189825 , 189826 and 189860 . Metal composition of the coin is: Cu 55.7065, Sn 4.1952, As 2.2783, Pb 36.7685, Fe 0.8302, Ni 0.1179, Zn,Sb,Cd,Bi,Co,Mn all are under detection and error limits, Sum 99.8966%, XRF data. Metal colour and composition are strong different from #33693. Zinc and stibium absent here, lead and tin contents elevated, copper content is lower more than 1/3. Apparently alloy is heterogeneous (liquated). Patination of the coin is phosphate type (up to 2.8 % P) and presumably represented by pyromorphite Pb5[PO4]3Cl. We can suppose, that this coin was made on another mint that Z# 33693 .

From my personal collection, I bought this around 2018 or so off of eBay. What is the correct attribution for this series of 'ash' runic square hole coins? Smirnova #1445. This type is attributed to Ferghana by Hartill in his GCC, #4.28, as well as by Michael Fedorov in his 2003 article "Money circulation in early-mediaeval Ustrushana, Farghana, and Tokharistan (6th - first half of 8th century AD)". Smirnova does not attribute it (to my limited knowledge) but she includes the findspots of Kuva, Ferghana, one from Bukhara, and three from Otrar. Smirnova also points out that this type had not been found Semirech'e. What is the reason for attributing it to Sayram here on Zeno? Is there more recent evidence that points to this? Fedorov suggests that the city of Osh in present-day Uzbekistan may be the meaning of the "Ash" or "Ush" runic letter. Is there any other evidence or theories? I wrote a thread about this coin on CoinTalk in 2019. It is mostly speculation and I did not really understand the series, nor the context for these Central Asian cash imitations, so I am sure that it is riddled with inaccuracies. At the time I was using Hartill and Smirnova's works and I landed on a conclusion of Ferghana, 627-649, by a local Göktürk ruler possibly named Kan Bagatur. Obv.: Malik Aram Yinal Chig (in Arab.) t-r-b-l Rev.: plain Metal composition of the coin is: Cu 78.41, Zn 7.29, Sn 11.32, As 0.35, Sb 1.16, Pb 0.85, Fe 0.33, Ni 0.18, Co below error level, Sum 99.90%, microprobe data in scanning mode on surface 30x20 mkm. So we have here very low-lead, zincian bronze of yellow colour. Atomic ratio Zn+Fe:Sn ~ 1:1 of the alloy is close to one in mineral kesterite ( https://www.mindat.org/min-2189.html ). Ores with kesterite could to be mined in Zeravshan or Inylchek ranges in Kyrgyzstan. Degradation of the alloy during alteration in ground is typical for bronzes. Leaching of Zn from the coins surface resulted not in redcashization (formation of red copper outer layer) typical for brasses, but silvery-white film of intermetallide Cu2Sn (well visible along the coin edge) was formed. Mineralization crust of the coin is oxide-carbonate type (tenorite + minium -> hydroromarchite -> cerussite) tell us, that the coin initially was burned in open flame and later was oxidized not deep in ground in cold fresh ground water.

This is a Central Asian imitation of Tang Dynasty square-holed coins with the legend ‘Kai-yuan Tong-bao’ (開元通寶). Unearthed in Chuy (Chui) region, Kyrgyzstan. Character 開 [kai] is written in ‘running’ script. For me it resembles the character 关 (関) [guan], but it is only my guess. The top element of character 寶 [bao] resembles the radical 山 [shan] – ‘mountain’. Element 貝 [bei] of character 寶 features several separated dots (with lines between them). Probably, this is a pictographic character representing the local landscape – mountains, stones and rivers. I invented a special Chinese term for this calligraphic variety: 山冠点贝宝 – “Character ‘bao’ with radical ‘shan’ on top and dots in radical ‘bei’.” The similar coin unearthed in the same area can be seen there: Zeno # 162023 .

The coin was unearthed at Krasnorechenskoe site (Kyrgyzstan), and apparently is local imitation of such coins issued in Xinjiang in Tang times. Compare with Z##696 and 697. These coins has distinctly yellow colour metal different from one of original Xinjiang issues. Compare also with Z# 223061 . Composition of metal of the coin also is uncommon: Cu 70.28, Sn 20.01, As 1.96, Pb 7.11, Fe 0.47, Ag,Zn,Sb,Bi,Co,Ni all are below detection or error levels, Sum 99.83%, microprobe data in scanning mode on surface 250x150 mkm. So we have here yellow As-bearing high-tin, low-lead bronze very different from usual for Xinjiang issues (cf. Z## 37794 , 44241 , 158424 and 172899 ) high-lead, moderately tin pinkish bronzes. Structure of this bronze also is very unusual and enigmatic for me - it is homogeneous on back-scattered electron images being heterogeneous compositionally. Point microprobe analysa gave wide deviations of main components Cu 85.22-74.32, Sn 11.54-15.54, As 1.25-2.32, Pb 0.00-7.44. But high-tin compositions (giving elevated tin content to alloy) weren't found. Besides that alloy don't contains desseminated pure lead drops so typical for Chinese lead bronzes structure. By other words the alloy was melted under very high temperatures and had cool very fast, what implys very different casting technology. Besides that the alloy is enriched with silver. Instead of lead drops it contains small (2-15 mkm) but abundant inclusions of pure silver. They are present not in metal itself, but in products of its alteration. This means, that the bronze contains silver in concentrations below sensitivity of microprobe 0.20% (only one point analysis gave 1.57% Ag), but during oxidation of base metals silver detached from alloy, concentrated and form its own phase. So we may conclude, that such coins are local Middle Asian production, imitations of Chinese Da Li YB, were cast by original technology from local raw materials. Personal collection item, so far an unique specimen. The excavation point of the coin is unknown as it was mixed with a hoard of dirhams from many time periods when being sold. This was the only early Medieval Semirech'e styled coinage in the mix. In my personal belief there are two main possibilities for the tamgha: one is that it is closely related to the wine-glass tamgha settlers in the 9th century, before the area's coinage was fully controlled by the Kara Khanids. Reason for this belief is that the wine-glass tamgha, when bottom part removed, becomes the current tamgha. Research by Babayarov 2019 presented at the Inner Mongolia University conference show that details are added to Turkic tamghas as local rulers seek to delineate their own rulership from that of the central khaganate or from other rulers. The similarity of this tamgha to ram horns from the Afrasiab murals is astonishing, possibly suggesting a Turkic connection. Krasnaya Rechka and Suyab are two locations that seem possible for the original casting of this coin, for the first has unearthed the wine glass tamgha coins and the latter has been the capital for the Western Turks, the Turgesh, and the Karluks, three main coin casters of Semirech'e known to cast in this style. A second possibility is that this coin's tamghas evolved from the Chinese character "元", which could be a result of Sino-Turko iconographic fusion. There is evidence that the character "元" has appeared on Turgesh coins from the Black Turgesh faction casted by ruler W'xswt'wy (recent research by numismatist Wu Zhonghua in his book "Turgesh Coinage" suggest that Turgesh coins were factionalized between Black and Yellow tribes, and that the Black tribe uses the runic tamgha while the Yellow uses the "X" tamgha). It is plausible that the character became a tamgha, though this in my personal belief is the less possible explanation. Given the effaced nature of the coin's obverse it is unclear who the issuers were. The late 9th century Arslanids have casted coinage with a reverse that has four tamghas, presented in Kamyshev 2002, and the tamghas also have possible ram horn elements. The connection is unclear, but the weight and design of both types of coinage is extremely similar.
